title: Cold-Hot Page Tiling and Retention Playbook for KV Cache
content:
Overview:

This playbook proposes a pragmatic, runtime-friendly memory layout and retention strategy for the KV cache that balances low-latency access for hot keys with long tail capacity for cold state, while minimizing fragmentation on long-lived GPU processes. The central idea is to organize cached entries into fixed-size pages grouped into variable-sized tiles and separate memory pools with explicit retention semantics (hot/warm/cold).

Goals:
- Keep the common short-sequence/affine-access case extremely fast (O(1) lookup & minimal allocation churn).
- Avoid large-scale compaction pauses; compaction should be incremental and backgrounded.
- Expose simple knobs to trade memory headroom vs tail quality for different customer SLAs (hosted API vs Dedicated).
- Make eviction decisions cheap and locality-aware (tile-level operations preferred over per-entry expensive scans).
- Provide observability and safe rollout path (canary, throttled compaction).

Terminology (definitions used in this doc):
- page: fixed-size allocation unit (base unit for GPU/CPU GLM pages). Suggested default: 64KB for GPU textures, tunable per-hardware class.
- tile: contiguous group of pages representing a logical locality bucket (e.g., single model shard KV prefix or session). Tiles are the primary unit for placement and coarse-grained eviction.
- slot: index within a page where a serialized KV entry lives (variable sized entries allowed; slot map keeps offsets).
- pool: named memory region (hot, warm, cold) with admission/eviction rules and accounting.
- retention window: time- or request-count-based threshold that determines when items are eligible for demotion/eviction.

High-level layout and invariants:
1) Fixed page size to reduce external fragmentation. Pages are carved out from large GPU allocations; avoid many tiny device allocations. Default page size 64KB, but allow 32KB/128KB profiles for different models.
2) Tiles are formed by grouping pages that likely share hotness (session affinity, shard id, recent co-access). Each tile tracks aggregate metadata: recent-access score (exponential decay), total used bytes, free bytes, and a per-tile LRU chain of slots (for intra-tile eviction).
3) Pools: hot, warm, cold. The hot pool contains tiles with the highest scores and gets placement priority. Warm is for transient reuse; cold retains long-tail entries but is subject to slower eviction and lower allocation priority.
4) Allocation flows: allocate in hot if tile score >= hot_threshold; otherwise warm. Cold pool allocation only happens when warm is saturated and a retention policy requires keeping tail entries (rare for typical latency-first ops).

Admission and eviction heuristics:
- Two-tier eviction: tile-level first, slot-level second. When the runtime needs to free memory, it prefers to evict entire cold tiles (bulk free) or demote hot tiles to warm, instead of scanning many slots. Bulk operations reduce metadata overhead and improve cacheline-friendly frees.
- Within a tile, use a bounded per-tile LRU with a small approximate counter to avoid per-access expensive operations. We maintain a 8-bit saturating recency counter per slot and periodically age counters instead of touching global LRU structures on every read to keep the hot path hot.
- Eviction scoring: primary factor is tile_score * tile_size_penalty + recency_penalty + workload_coherence_boost. This favors evicting large, cold tiles before smaller but moderately used tiles.
- Demotion policy: items first move hot->warm after their decayed score falls below hot_threshold, then warm->cold after a longer window. Cold entries are scanned only on explicit low-priority background compaction or when absolutely needed for allocation.

Memory pool internals and fragmentation mitigation:
- Use segregated page freelists by page size and pool. Each page keeps a small header with occupancy bitmap to allow quick allocation of variable-size slots without splitting pages at allocation time (internal fragmentation bounded by page granularity).
- Avoid slab-only designs; instead use hybrid slabless pooling where larger serialized KV blobs can be allocated as contiguous slots across pages in the same tile using a small vector of page indices (multi-page mapping). This reduces large-object fragmentation and expensive copy-on-compact.
- Incremental compaction: background worker picks high-fragmentation tiles (based on free_fraction + average slot slack) and compacts them by evacuating live slots into freshly allocated pages. Compact passes are rate-limited and can be canceled if load increases. Compaction prefers to compact warm->cold candidate tiles first.
- Buddy sub-allocator for CPU-side staging memory at page granularity to quickly satisfy short-term bursts and reduce device allocation churn.

Interaction with scheduler and kernels:
- Scheduler hints: Serving runtime scheduler will annotate requests with expected sequence length and priority. Tile admission uses these hints to prefetch or pin pages for expected upcoming steps (e.g., for streaming generation we pin the top-k current tokens’ KV in hot pool).
- Kernel-friendly layout: pages are aligned to kernel-preferred block sizes and memory accesses for evict/restore paths are contiguous to maximize DMA throughput. Page headers are structured to allow O(1) restore of a contiguous range to a kernel's KV cache region.

Observability and metrics to expose:
- per_pool_total_bytes, per_pool_used_bytes, per_pool_free_pages
- tile_count_by_pool, avg_tile_fragmentation_ratio, tiles_marked_for_compaction
- eviction_ops_total {reason=bulk|slot|demote|compaction}
- avg_slot_internal_slack, large_object_spans_count
- compaction_time_ms_p50_p95, compaction_canceled_counts
- allocation_latency_ms_p50_p95
- admission_rejection_count (how often allocation forced eviction)

Config knobs (defaults and ranges):
- page_size: 32KB|64KB|128KB (default 64KB)
- hot_threshold: float [0,1] (default 0.7)
- warm_window_seconds: int (default 120)
- compaction_rate_limit_bytes_per_sec: int (default 64MB/s)
- max_hot_pool_fraction: float (default 0.6)

Example runtime config snippet (pseudo YAML):

cache:
  page_size: 65536
  pools:
    hot: {max_fraction: 0.6, admission_threshold: 0.7}
    warm: {max_fraction: 0.25}
    cold: {max_fraction: 0.15, eviction_bias: bulk}
  compaction: {enabled: true, rate_limit_bytes_per_sec: 67108864}

Operational playbook (canary -> rollout):
1) Start with warm-only mode: hot pool disabled. Observe allocation latency and tail quality for small workloads.
2) Enable hot pool on canary fleet (5% traffic) with conservative hot_threshold. Watch admission_rejection_count and allocation latency.
3) Enable compaction background worker at low rate. Verify compaction_time_ms and compaction_canceled_counts.
4) Gradually increase hot pool fraction and lower hot_threshold for latency-sensitive tiers.

Runbook for on-call:
- Rapid OOMs: inspect per_pool_free_pages and eviction_ops_total; if bulk eviction spiked, increase compaction rate or temporarily increase cold pool fraction.
- Latency regressions: check allocation_latency_ms_p95 and admission_rejection_count; consider increasing hot_pool fraction or pre-pin critical tiles.
- Compaction stalls: check compaction_canceled_counts and CPU/GPU scheduling; back off compaction rate if it correlates with CPU saturation.

Experiments to validate choices (A/B candidates):
- Compare page_size 32KB vs 64KB vs 128KB under two workloads: short-session chat (hundreds of tiny entries) and long-context summarization (few very large blobs). Metrics: p99 latency, mem efficiency, compaction overhead.
- Evaluate bulk-tile-eviction vs per-slot LRU under synthetic skewed-access traces (Zipf alpha sweep). Measure CPU overhead and eviction churn.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How to best co-locate tiles across GPUs for multi-GPU models with cross-shard KV sharing? Naive tiling can cause cross-device duplication.
- When is it beneficial to allow limited tail replication in hot pool (for heavy read OLAP-like workloads) vs strict single-copy semantics?
- Should compaction be eviction-aware (i.e., proactively compress rarely-read values) or purely relocation-focused?

Appendix: short checklist before merging to main runtime branch:
- unit tests for tile-level eviction and tile demotion path
- microbench harness for allocation latency and compaction throughput
- example dashboard (Grafana) panels for new metrics
- a canary plan with traffic % and rollback criteria (OOM rate, p95 latency increase > 10%)

This playbook is intended as a concrete starting point and not the final design. The next step is to convert the hot/warm/cold pool concepts into a small prototype in the serving-runtime feature branch and run the microbench experiments listed above.
